versions.text:
The Owl Who Counted Stars

High in an old oak tree, at the edge of a quiet orchard, lived a little owl named Mabel.

Evening came softly. The sun slipped down behind the apple trees. The sky turned from gold to pink, and then to a deep, soft blue.

Mabel fluffed her feathers. "It is time," she whispered.

She climbed down from her high branch, one careful step at a time. Her round house was warm inside. It smelled of cedar wood and dried lavender.

First, she made her cocoa. She poured warm milk into a small blue cup. She stirred it three times, slowly. Clink, clink, clink went the spoon. Then she sipped. It tasted sweet and creamy.

Next, she tidied her shelf. She set her wooden bird a little straighter. She patted her soft pillow twice. Pat, pat. Then she opened the window just a crack, so the cool night air could drift in.

Now came her favorite part. She pulled her patchwork quilt from the hook by the door. It was made of many squares. There were red squares, green squares, and squares the color of butter. Each one had been stitched by hand, long ago, by her grandmother.

Mabel wrapped the quilt around her shoulders. It felt heavy and warm, like a sleepy cat curled up in her lap.

She climbed onto the window seat. The wood was smooth under her feet. Outside, the orchard was quiet. The apple trees stood still, like friendly giants resting their arms.

From far away came a soft sound. Hoo. Hoo. It was another owl, calling goodnight to the world.

Mabel smiled. "Goodnight, Owl," she called back, very softly.

Then she looked up. One small star blinked into view above the orchard.

"One," Mabel counted quietly.

Another star appeared, bright and faraway. "Two."

Then a third, just over the tallest apple tree. "Three."

The stars came out one by one, as if they were waking up for the night. "Four. Five."

A gentle breeze moved through the leaves. Whish, whish, it sang, like a lullaby being hummed. "Six."

The moon rose slowly over the hill. It was round and silver and calm. It looked down at Mabel as if to say hello. "Seven," she whispered. "Hello, Moon."

The moon glowed a little brighter, just for her.

"Eight," Mabel murmured. Her eyes were getting heavy now. Her blinks were getting slower.

"Nine." The quilt felt warmer. The window seat felt softer. The air smelled of apples and lavender and night.

"Ten," Mabel breathed, and her head drooped gently to one side.

She did not finish counting the rest. The stars kept shining anyway, every one of them, keeping watch over the orchard.

Mabel tucked her feet under her quilt. She rested her cheek against the cool glass. The last of the cocoa warmed her tummy.

Hoo, called the far-off owl, very softly now. Hoo.

Mabel's eyes closed. Her feathers rose and fell, rose and fell, slow and steady. The quilt hugged her close, square by square.

Outside, the moon kept its quiet watch, and the stars twinkled on, and the orchard slept.

Goodnight, little owl.

Mabel makes choices (cocoa, tidying, greeting the moon and the other owl).

versions.text:
Tomas and the Silver Whistle

In a green meadow, where the grass grew tall, there was a small den under an old oak tree. Tomas the young fox lived there with his grandmother.

Grandmother Fern had a silver whistle. Every evening she blew it, and the birds flew home to roost. Tiny chirps came from every bush.

One day, the whistle was gone.

"Oh dear," said Grandmother Fern. She looked under her blanket. She looked behind the teapot. "I think I dropped it when I went to pick berries."

Tomas puffed out his chest. "Don't worry, Grandma. I will find it for you!"

Grandmother Fern smiled. "Thank you, my brave little fox. Be careful, and come back before the stars come out."

Tomas trotted out of the den. The sun was warm on his orange fur. He walked along the path toward the reed pond.

The reeds swayed and whispered. Tomas stopped at the edge of the water. He saw ducks paddling in circles.

"Excuse me," Tomas called. "Have you seen a silver whistle?"

A duck named Pip turned around. "We saw something shiny near the mud. But the water is too deep for a fox to cross."

Tomas looked at the water. It was deep, but a row of flat stones poked up in a line. They looked like steppingstones.

"I can hop from stone to stone," Tomas said. "I will go slowly."

He took one careful step. Then another. Then a big hop to the last stone. He landed with a soft thump on the other side.

"Hooray!" quacked Pip. "You did it!"

Tomas searched the muddy bank. But there was no whistle. Only a shiny pebble.

He sighed. Then he remembered what Grandma always said: "When you are stuck, look up and see the path."

Tomas looked up. Far away, on a hill, he saw a field of wildflowers. Something silver glinted in the grass.

Tomas climbed the hill one paw at a time. The flowers tickled his nose. Purple, yellow, and pink petals swayed in the breeze.

But near the top, he came to a patch of tangled thorny vines. A little rabbit was stuck beneath them.

"Help, please!" squeaked the rabbit. "I went looking for clover, and now I cannot get out."

Tomas thought hard. He nosed the vines gently to the left, then to the right. He pulled one loose strand at a time, very softly.

"There you go," said Tomas. "Easy does it."

The rabbit hopped free. "Thank you, kind fox! I am Clover. Let me help you look."

Together they searched the hilltop. Clover spotted it first. Tomas saw the silver shine poking out from under a mossy stone.

He pulled it out gently with his teeth. The whistle was cool and smooth.

"We found it!" cheered Clover.

Tomas and Clover walked back down the hill. The sky turned peach and then soft blue. Golden light faded from the meadow.

They passed the reed pond. Pip the duck waved a wing. The frogs began to hum a sleepy song.

Tomas crept into the den. Grandmother Fern sat in her rocking chair, her eyes bright.

"You found it!" she whispered.

Tomas held up the whistle. "I did, Grandma. And I made a friend too."

Grandmother Fern hugged him close. "You are a good fox, Tomas."

She tucked a warm blanket around him. The den smelled of pine and clover. Outside, the last birds settled into their nests.

Grandma did not blow the whistle tonight. The birds were already home.

Tomas yawned a big, wide yawn. His eyes grew heavy.

"Goodnight, Grandma," he murmured.

"Goodnight, little fox," said Grandmother Fern softly.

And the meadow grew quiet, and Tomas fell fast asleep.

safety.evidence: Tomas hops across deep water on flat stones, a fox wanders off alone along a path, and he climbs a hill and pulls loose thorny vines. No injury or scary images; the water crossing is done alone without a grown-up, which is a copyable unsafe act.
safety.fix: In the reed pond paragraph, have Tomas call for Grandma or another grown-up before crossing, or remove the stepping-stone crossing and have him walk around the pond instead.

versions.text:
Pip and the Tallest Hedgehog

Pip the hedgehog had a big wish. He wanted to be the tallest hedgehog in the whole garden.

"I will be the tallest!" said Pip. He puffed out his prickles and stood up as straight as he could.

But Pip was short. Very, very short.

"Hmm," said Pip. "I need to be taller. I know! I will stack things!"

Pip went to the tea table. He carefully stacked one teacup on top of another. Then another. Then another.

Clink, clink, clonk!

"Look at me!" said Pip. He climbed up, wobble, wobble, wobble. He stood on the very top teacup.

Splish! Splash! The teacups tipped over, and Pip tumbled into a bed of soft moss.

"Oops," said Pip, with a little giggle. "That was a bumpy try!"

Pip shook off his prickles and tried again. This time he went to the garden shed. He rolled out the flower pots, one by one. Big pots, little pots, round pots, and one shiny pot with a dent.

Pip stacked the pots higher and higher. Boing! Boing! Boing!

Then Pip spotted his friend Hattie the toad sitting by the water pond.

"Hattie!" called Pip. "Come and help me be tall!"

Hattie hopped over with a bright, cheery "Ribbit!" She hopped right onto the top pot.

"Okay, Pip," said Hattie. "Now you climb on my back!"

Pip climbed up, up, up, scrambling onto Hattie's bumpy back. He wobbled. He teetered. He stood up on his tiptoes.

Whoosh! Splat! Pots went rolling everywhere, and Pip and Hattie landed in a big, soft heap of grass.

"Ribbit!" laughed Hattie. "That was the silliest thing I have ever seen!"

Pip laughed so hard that his prickles shook. "Hattie, I'm still not tall," he giggled.

"That's okay," said Hattie. "Let's try one more time. But this time, let's do it together."

Pip thought for a moment. Then he had a happy idea. He ran off to the garden gate and came back with a big, fluffy pillow from the swing.

"Ta-da!" said Pip. "This is the tallest pillow in the garden!"

Hattie hopped onto the pillow. Pip climbed on top of Hattie. Then Pip stood up very, very carefully.

Puff! The pillow squished and bounced. Pip wobbled, and Hattie wobbled, and they both laughed and laughed until they had to sit down again.

Then Pip and Hattie stopped wobbling. They sat side by side on the soft, cozy pillow. They looked up at the big, wide sky.

"Pip," said Hattie quietly, "from down here, we can see the clouds."

Pip looked up. A fluffy white cloud floated slowly past, shaped like a sleepy bear.

"It's the best view in the garden," said Pip. He smiled a big, sleepy smile.

The garden grew quiet. The breeze whispered through the flowers. The bees hummed softly. The sky turned gold and pink.

Hattie yawned a wide, slow yawn. "Ribbit," she sighed. "I think I'm getting sleepy."

"Me too," said Pip, and he curled up his prickles into a round, warm ball. "Goodnight, Hattie."

"Goodnight, Pip," whispered Hattie. "You're the tallest friend I know."

And the two friends snuggled down on the pillow, listening to the quiet garden, and drifted off to sleep under the soft, glowing sky.
